newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Papua New Guinea PM replaces army chief - radio.
newsitem.headline: Papua New Guinea PM replaces army chief - radio.

text.p: Papua New Guinea Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan, in another concession to those calling for his resignation, has replaced Colonel Alfred Aikung as head of the army, Australian Broadcasting Corp radio reported on Monday.

Chan appointed Aikung last Tuesday after firing army chief Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok, who had called for Chan's resignation over the prime minister's hiring of mercenaries to help fight secessionist rebels on the island of Bougainville.

"He (Aikung) has now been replaced by General Jack Tuat who is the Defence Force chief of staff ... and importantly it's known that General Singirok was consulted in the course of the change," the ABC reported.
Aikung, originally from PNG's tiny navy, was unpopular with the army and his authority was never recognised by troops who remained loyal to Singirok.

The army revolt began last Monday when Singirok said a US$36 million contract with British-based military consultancy Sandline International, which provided 70 mercenaries, was unlawful and that those involved were corrupt.
He called for Chan and other senior ministers to resign within 48 hours or be forced aside by the people.
Street protests in support of the rebel officers erupted into two days of violence and looting in Port Moresby after Singirok's sacking. But tight security has since restored calm.

All the mercenaries except their leader, former British Colonel Tim Spicer, have left the country after the government suspended their contract. Spicer was due to appear in court on Monday to face firearms charges.
Opposition political leaders on Sunday said they would move a motion in parliament on Tuesday requesting Chan to resign.
Chan's replacement of Aikung is another concession to the army, after Chan's suspension of the contract with the mercenaries and the appointment of an inquiry into the contract.
However, Chan he has yet to make the final concession demanded by the troops -- his own resignation.
Chan declared in national television address late on Sunday that he would not resign.
